You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.

# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly show at least one frog placed within the toilet, rather than merely on its lid, rim, or nearby floor?
node.criteria: Pass if at least one frog is visibly situated within the toilet bowl interior, with spatial cues such as its position relative to the bowl opening and rim, contact, or occlusion supporting that it is inside rather than perched on the rim or merely overlapping the opening. Fail if the visible evidence establishes that no frog is placed within the toilet. Unknown if the relevant spatial relation cannot be resolved from the image. A frog on the lid, rim, or nearby floor alone does not establish placement within the toilet; additional frogs in those locations do not negate a genuine placement within it.
node.binding: Assess placement within the toilet shown in the edited image; do not require a particular number of frogs beyond at least one, and do not treat mere overlap with the toilet as placement within it.

node_traces.evidence: A frog is visibly situated inside the toilet bowl, below the rim and within the bowl opening. Other frogs on the lid and nearby floor do not negate this placement.

fulfillment: The node’s binding is too abbreviated and omits the reference-to-edit comparison, so it may be treating any visible frog in the bowl as proof that the requested edit was completed. In the source, a small dark object is already visible in the bowl; the edited image adds a clear frog there, but also adds frogs on the lid and floor. The trace’s bowl-placement observation is credible evidence of progress, not by itself evidence that the requested change is complete. Preserve the criterion that a frog be inside the bowl, but make the decision use the saved source-relative support observations and distinguish a newly added placement from a pre-existing object or ambiguous placement. Do not count the lid/floor frogs as progress or as negating the bowl frog, and do not impose a frog-count or cleanup requirement. The reference is partial, but it constrains only the aggregate: investigate why the current complete/yes path disagrees rather than hard-coding partial or treating the skipped s2 as negative evidence. Keep conditional skips distinct from failed observations; if the source-relative evidence cannot resolve completion, retain uncertainty rather than inferring absence from low confidence or missing support.
